text: Your report is written and your presentations built. This lesson is about turning that finished work into something that actually functions as a portfolio piece — discoverable, well-documented, and genuinely useful when someone unfamiliar with your project looks at it for the first time.

This lesson covers what a portfolio-ready capstone repository actually needs beyond the code, how to write a README that lets a stranger understand your project in under two minutes, how to package your report, presentation, and data so each is independently useful, and how this packaging step connects directly to Chapter 6's career preparation.

A repository containing only raw code is your working files, not yet a portfolio piece. A portfolio-ready version adds a README that orients a first-time visitor, the written report as a readable document rather than buried in code comments, both your technical and non-specialist presentation slides, and your final dataset and run log, ideally with a note on how to regenerate your analysis if someone wanted to check your work.

A worked portfolio structure: a README at the root, a report folder with the final report as a PDF, a slides folder with both the technical and general-audience talks, a data folder with the run log and raw results, and a source folder with the circuit, noise-scaling, and extrapolation code. This structure makes the project legible to three different visitors: a hiring manager skimming the README and report, a technical interviewer opening the slides and code, and someone trying to verify or extend your work.

A strong README answers, near the very top: what question did this project investigate, in one sentence; what was found, in one or two sentences with the actual headline number; and how is the repository organized, a short list of folders. Everything else — full methodology, detailed limitations, setup instructions — comes after this orienting summary, not before it.

Chapter 6's lessons on portfolio-building and interview preparation assume you have something exactly like this structure ready to point to. Next lesson closes this chapter: having someone else read your draft critically, and actually revising based on what they find.
